claims.text: Above 900 °C, formation and persistence of a protective oxide layer in CrFeCoNiX alloys is governed by alloy composition.
The Cr-to-Fe ratio is the specific compositional variable governing protective-oxide behavior.
Changing the Cr-to-Fe ratio changes the oxide layer's crystal structure.
Changing the Cr-to-Fe ratio changes the oxide layer's defect density.
The oxide layer's crystal structure governs its formation and persistence.
The oxide layer's defect density governs its formation and persistence.
Thermodynamic principles govern oxide-layer formation and stability.
Kinetic principles govern oxide-layer formation and stability.
An appropriate Cr-to-Fe ratio will produce a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide with a thickness-growth rate below 10 μm/h.
CrFeCoNiX alloys having a Cr-to-Fe ratio of 1:1 develop unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation.
The unstable 1:1 Cr-to-Fe baseline has an oxide thickness-growth rate of 50 μm/h.
The proposed behavior applies to single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys.
The proposed behavior applies above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
The exact relationship between Cr-to-Fe ratio, oxide crystal structure, and oxide defect density is not well understood.
The roles of Si, Mn, and Al in the proposed mechanism are unclear.

contradictions.description: The claimed service boundary is above 900 °C, but both the proposed intervention and falsification experiment specify testing at exactly 900 °C, which does not test the stated boundary.

The baseline asserts a 50 μm/h growth rate for a 1:1 Cr-to-Fe CrFeCoNiX alloy, while the falsification rule says that any CrFeCoNiX composition exceeding 20 μm/h falsifies the hypothesis. Thus, the stated baseline itself meets the stated falsification condition.
